newsitem.title: UK: Wary UK funds see continued Wall Street volatility.
newsitem.headline: Wary UK funds see continued Wall Street volatility.

text.p: UK-based fund managers are treading softly after Monday's Wall Street plunge, saying the market was overdue a correction and will experience continued volatility, but with few signs of a profound change in direction in the medium term.
"The market has been at the extreme positive end of the sentiment and valuation spectrum," said Hilary Speller, fund manager at Gartmore of a $1.8 billion U.S. portfolio.
"It is vulnerable to these sort of shakeouts but I don't think this is a fundamental change (in direction)."
Dow Jones industrials tumbled 192 points, or 2.5 percent, on Monday after Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto raised the possibility of Japan selling U.S. government bonds to buy gold.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said Tuesday that Hashimoto's remarks had been incorrectly reported and that Japan had no intention of dumping U.S. Treasuries.
Fund managers generally discounted Hashimoto's remarks Tuesday.

"If the whole trade picture and capital flows switch direction, that would be a major factor. But, what we are seeing is the usual amount of trade tensions that exist between the U.S. and Japan," Speller said.

"At the end of the day, it is a threat. Markets have worries and they have hopes, but that is not what causes cash flows," said Gareth Watts, a fund manager at John Govett & Co, with a $400 million portfolio of U.S. securities.
U.S. stocks and bonds would be hit if Japanese investments were repatriated, fund managers said, but they attributed much of yesterday's fall to volatility and a predisposition to a correction.
"The market was due to come back, it hadn't had a breather in some time," said Watts. "When there is a lot of optimism around you only need something small to send it down."
Though U.S. equities look overvalued from a historic standpoint, fund managers said, in the absence of any hard evidence of a Japanese pullback any effect would be short-lived.
"We haven't had a significant shift in either the inflation or earnings outlook for the equity market and therefore I don't think a major correction downward is likely," Speller said.

Jenny Hayward, a manager of U.S. funds at Edinburgh Fund Managers, said that regardless of a retraction by the Japanese, Hashimoto's remarks were an external shock that might serve "to put the overvaluation of the market into perspective."
The influx of Japanese money has been crucial to the spectacular performance of U.S. stock markets, fund managers noted.
"The strength of the U.S. markets in the past two years have been heavily underpinned by Japanese buying of Treasuries," Hayward said.

The Japanese have kept domestic interest rates extremely low, fund managers said, in part to aid an ailing economy but also to allow the troubled banking sector to benefit from a wide spread between funding and lending rates.

This, in turn, has caused yield-seeking Japanese investors to pile into U.S. Treasuries, keeping interest rates in the U.S. relatively low and making the stock markets more attractive to U.S. investors.

If Japanese money were to pull back from U.S. Treasuries, fund managers said, the effect likely would be a rise in interest rates to attract more capital to fill the gap - probably from the stock market.
But for now fund managers are playing down the danger of this actually happening.
"The idea of (Japan) switching into gold seems a little strange to me, being a non-interest bearing commodity," Speller said.
